query: For multiprincipal-element alloys intended for sustained use in harsh high-temperature environments, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs oxidation resistance and material integrity, and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the range over which the hypothesis should hold, relevant supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In multiprincipal-element alloys containing moderate-to-high Al and Cr content, the dominant factor governing oxidation resistance and material integrity at 800–1200 °C is the synergistic formation of a stable, continuous, protective oxide scale (predominantly Al2O3 and/or Cr2O3) that suppresses both inward oxygen diffusion and outward metal transport, thereby preserving structural soundness under long-term exposure.
generation.material_initial_state: A series of baseline equiatomic multiprincipal-element alloys (e.g., FeNiCuAl-based or CrMnFeCoNi variants) cast or powder-processed under similar conditions, with uniform initial chemistry prior to systematic compositional variation in Al/Cr ratio.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary Al and/or Cr content in the alloy from low to moderate/high levels, while keeping other elements in near-equimolar proportions. Conduct high-temperature oxidation tests, microstructural characterization (e.g., SEM, TEM, XRD), and atomistic simulations to evaluate the formation and stability of oxide scales and underlying phases.
generation.conditions: Expose each alloy variant to oxidizing atmospheres (e.g., air or controlled oxygen partial pressure) at 800–1200 °C for prolonged durations representative of service conditions (e.g., tens to hundreds of hours), with periodic or in situ characterization.
generation.structural_mediator: Primary oxide scale formation governed by the transport of Al and Cr to the alloy surface, resulting in the nucleation and growth of dense, adherent Al2O3/Cr2O3 phases at high temperatures.
generation.mechanism: The protective oxide scale forms more quickly and remains stable in alloys with higher Al/Cr, limiting both outward diffusion of metal ions and inward penetration of oxygen. This reduces internal oxidation, maintains the alloy’s structural integrity, and diminishes spallation over time.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to low-Al/Cr alloys, those with optimized Al/Cr levels will exhibit lower mass gain during isothermal weight-gain tests, thicker and more continuous protective oxide layers on cross-sectional microscopy, and reduced spallation or cracking in cyclic oxidation tests.
generation.baseline: An alloy composition with minimal Al and Cr content that forms discontinuous or multi-layered, less stable oxide scales at high temperature, leading to higher mass gains and scale spallation over long exposures.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for polycrystalline multiprincipal-element alloys containing Al and Cr in near-equimolar elemental distributions, under oxidizing conditions between 800 and 1200 °C for extended times. Beyond these ranges, other factors (e.g., phases formed by additional elements, volatile species, or mechanical loading) may introduce different mechanisms of degradation.
generation.uncertainty: Exact Al/Cr ratios required for optimal oxidation resistance may vary depending on other alloying elements and specific service environments. Further experiments and modeling are needed to refine the precise composition ranges and clarify long-term stability under thermal cycling.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three alloy sets with systematically increased Al/Cr content (e.g., 5 at.%, 10 at.%, 15 at.% each) while keeping other elements in near-equimolar proportions, and subject them alongside a low-Al/Cr reference alloy to isothermal and cyclic oxidation at 800–1200 °C. In parallel, perform atomistic simulations with the same compositions and experimental conditions to predict oxide structure and growth kinetics.
measurements: Phase and microstructure (XRD, SEM, TEM, cross-sectional EDS).
Element diffusion profiles via atom probe tomography or related methods.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: Observing no correlation between Al/Cr content and the development of stable protective oxide scales (i.e., no significant differences in oxide composition, microstructure, or mass change behaviors) would falsify the hypothesis.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, CrMnFeCoNi HEA behaviour responding to changes in temperature and environmental factors such as the partial pressure of oxygen has been investigated by in situ XRD at high temperatures up to 1100 °C. In situ thermal observations of materials with the high-temperature XRD provide unique information such as temperature-dependent phase transformations, types of new phase formation, and the start and finish temperatures of competing phases in an alloy system []. In situ HTXRD is instrumental in revealing the real-time of oxide formation as well as the type and temperature at which various kinds of oxide form when metals are exposed to high temperatures in air or in another simulated environment. Our HTXRD analysis provided insight into the thermal stability, phase transitions, and high-temperature oxidation behaviour of the CrMnFeCoNi alloy samples, which provides significant guidance in the development of high-performance alloys for demanding applications. The surface and cross-sectional microstructure, elemental distributions, and oxide compositions have been examined to further understand the evolution of the oxides. Among the various HEA systems, FeNiCuAl-based alloys are of particular interest because they combine relatively low raw-material cost with favorable overall performance. However, their insufficient oxidation resistance at temperatures of 900 °C and above remains a major obstacle to practical high-temperature applications [,,]. During oxidation, alloy durability is largely determined by the composition, compactness, adhesion, and growth kinetics of the surface oxide scale [,,]. In particular, the formation of a dense, continuous, and strongly adherent protective scale is essential for suppressing inward oxygen diffusion and outward metal-cation transport, thereby slowing oxidation and preventing premature scale failure [,,]. Alloying is an effective approach for improving the oxidation resistance of FeNiCuAl-based HEAs [,,]. Cr and Al are well known to promote the formation of thermodynamically stable Cr2O3 and Al2O3 protective scales, respectively, whereas Co can facilitate spinel formation and Mn can promote the development of MnCr2O4 while improving scale integrity and adhesion [,,]. chosen.why: A combined experimental and simulation study directly addresses the open mechanistic question of what governs oxidation resistance and structural integrity in multiprincipal-element alloys under harsh, high-temperature conditions. By systematically varying the composition (e.g., Al and Cr content), measuring oxide-scale evolution via thermogravimetry and microscopy, performing high-temperature mechanical tests, and carrying out atomistic simulations, one can derive a robust explanation of how protective oxide formation and microstructural stability dictate alloy performance and durability. Both experimental and modeling insights are crucial to confirm or falsify the mechanism, making this an approach well-suited to the question posed.
